inline.s: In truth, true and false are one substance, and living beings and Buddha are not two. Birth and death, nirvana, bodhi, and affliction are all the original mind and original nature; there is no need to discriminate, no need to delight or loathe, no need to grasp or reject. This mind is pure, fundamentally Buddha; it requires not a single dharma. How much chatter there is here — investigate!
(Recorded from Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions
· the Chan Hall Instructions

blocks.text: At First There Is No Huatou

inline.s: The ancient patriarchs pointed directly to the human mind, so that one sees the nature and becomes Buddha. Such as the first patriarch Damo’s settling of the mind, and the Sixth Patriarch’s talking solely of seeing the nature — one had only to accept it directly and that was enough;
there was no looking at a huatou

. By the time of the later patriarchs, they saw that the human heart was no longer upright, that men could not be dead-sincere but were full of cleverness, often counting the treasures of others as their own family jewels. So they had no choice but to each establish a gate, each put forth their own eye, and only then had students look at a huatou.

There are many topics, such as “The ten thousand dharmas return to one — to where does the one return?” or “Before my father and mother were born, what was my original face?” and so forth; but “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” is the most common.
What is a huatou? Hua is to speak, and tou is before speaking. For instance, reciting “Amitabha Buddha” is a spoken phrase,
and before it is spoken is the huatou
. The so-called huatou is the moment when a single thought has not yet arisen;
the instant a thought arises, it has already become the huashu

. This moment when a thought has not yet arisen is called non-arising; not being scattered, not being drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness — that is called non-ceasing. At every moment, with a single solitary thought, turn the light back and shine upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing”;
this is called looking at the huatou
, or tending the huatou.
To look at the huatou, one must first arouse the doubt;

the doubt is the staff of the huatou. What is the doubt? For instance, when one asks who it is who recites the Buddha’s name, everyone knows it is oneself reciting. But is it recited with the mouth, or with the mind? If it is with the mouth, when one is asleep the mouth is still there — why does it not recite? If it is with the mind, what does the mind look like? There is nowhere to grasp hold of it, and so one does not understand. Therefore, on the “who,” one rouses a slight
doubt-thought
, but it must not be coarse; the finer it is the better. At every time, in every place,
solely tend this single doubt-thought

, looking on as steadily as flowing water, without a second thought arising. If the doubt-thought is present, do not stir it; if it is not present, gently raise it again. When one first applies the mind, it is certain that in stillness one gains more strength than in movement; but on no account should one give rise to a discriminative mind. Do not concern yourself with whether you gain strength or not, and do not concern yourself with whether it is in movement or in stillness; just apply your work single-heartedly
[To look at the huatou, one must first arouse the doubt]
Then, how does one rouse the doubt? Old Master Xuyun said: “Start from the huashu.” In his Two Replies to Layman Jin Hongshu (

), Old Master Xuyun said: “If a beginner applies effort, he must of necessity pursue from the huashu. For in the Dharma-ending age, sentient beings have deep hindrances and shallow wisdom; without beginning from the huashu they cannot reach the huatou; without applying effort at the mind that has thought, they cannot realize the mind without thought.” In the Warning Words on Chan Practice, Old Master Xuyun said: “If you have not yet looked at the huatou (the head before the words), and your deluded thoughts and drowsiness are many, you should still look at the ‘who’ of ‘who is reciting the Buddha’s name.’ When you have seen that deluded thoughts and drowsiness have diminished, and the ‘who’ cannot be forgotten, then look at the place where this thought arises. When a thought does not arise at all, that is non-arising; to be able to see the thought’s non-arising is called truly looking at the huatou.”

Of the four words ‘who is reciting the Buddha’s name,’ the stress falls most heavily on the single word ‘who.’ The other three words only sketch the outline. For instance: who is it that dresses and eats? Who is it that defecates and urinates? Who is it that gives rise to ignorance? Who is it that can know and be aware? Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, once the ‘who’ is raised, it is most easy for the doubt-thought to arise, without waiting for repeated reflection and speculation to bring it about. Hence the ‘who’ as a huatou is truly a wonderful method of Chan practice.”

But this is not to recite the character ‘who’ or the four words ‘who is reciting the Buddha’s name’ as a Buddha-name, nor to reflect and speculate in search of who it is that recites — that is called the doubt. There are those
(some people)

who chant the four words ‘who is reciting the Buddha’s name’ without stopping; that is not as meritorious as reciting a thought of Amitabha Buddha. There are those who indulge in wild and confused thinking, searching here and there, and call that the doubt; little do they know that the more they think, the more numerous the deluded thoughts become — just as one who wishes to rise instead falls; this must be known.

The doubt-thought arouse by a beginner is very coarse. Breaking off and continuing, now ripe and now raw, it cannot be reckoned the doubt — it may only be called thinking. Gradually the wild mind is gathered in, and the thought can be held a little;
only then is it called probing

. Then gradually the effort matures, and one doubts without intending to doubt, no longer aware of where one sits, nor of body, mind, and world; a single doubt-thought is present, unbroken and unceasing;
only then is it called the doubt
. In truth, at the beginning how could that be counted as applying effort? It was merely making deluded thoughts.
Only when to this point the true doubt
(the genuine doubt-thought — thought after thought, without break, probing back toward the moment before a thought has sprouted)
comes present
, is it time for truly applying effort.
At this point there is a great pass, and one very easily runs into the wrong road

[Pass (ai)] An important strategic pass. [At this point there is a great pass] This is a great dangerous pass. When the effort has reached “disregarding the doubt and yet doubting of itself, no longer aware of where one sits, nor knowing body, mind, and world; a single doubt-thought present, unbroken and unceasing,” then the following clear and pure states appear. If one cannot handle them correctly, one easily runs into the wrong road.

One: at this point it is clear and pure, of infinite ease. If one loses bare awareness for a moment, one sinks into a state of light drowsiness. If a person with clear eyes were beside one, he would see at a glance that one is in this very state; one blow of the incense-board, and then the clouds and mists scatter at once, and many on account of this would awaken to the Way.

Two: at this point it is clear and pure, empty and hollow. If the doubt has vanished, then it is non-recollection — sitting on the withered-wood cliff, or what is called “soaking a stone in cold water.” When one reaches this point one must raise,
and to raise is bare awareness

. Awareness is not being deluded, which is prajna; reflection is not being scattered, which is samadhi. This single solitary thought, clear and still, reflecting, unmoving as suchness, luminous and undimmed, ever knowing — like a dying fire sending up smoke, a single thread stretching on without breaking.
[This single solitary thought] This single solitary thought of bare reflection.
When one’s effort reaches this point, one must have the diamond eye,
and no longer raise

; to raise is to put a head on top of a head. Formerly a monk asked the Aged Master Zhaozhou, saying: “When not even a single thing is brought along, what then?” Zhaozhou said: “Put it down.” The monk said: “If not even a single thing is brought along, what is there to put down?” Zhaozhou said: “If you cannot put it down, take it up and carry it.” This is precisely that moment. The scenery within is like a man drinking water — he alone knows whether it is warm or cold; it is not something that speech can reach. One who has come to this point naturally understands; one who has not come to this point, though one speak, it does no good. As the saying goes: “Meeting a swordsman, one must present the sword; if he is not a poet, do not offer him a poem.”
[When one’s effort reaches this point] When one’s effort has reached

the point of “this single solitary thought, clear and still, reflecting, unmoving as suchness, luminous and undimmed, ever knowing — like a dying fire sending up smoke, a single thread stretching on without breaking.” [No longer raising] At this time, though one no longer raises bare awareness, its reflection is still present, reflecting of itself — this is called still reflection. Still yet ever reflecting; reflecting yet ever still. Master Dayu’s verse says: “Still reflection, reflecting stillness — beware of using force. To become Buddha and be master, there is no other secret.” This speaks precisely of the state of still reflection.

blocks.text: The Instructions of My Grandteacher, the Venerable Master

inline.s: Recorded from
Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions
In the thirty-sixth year of the Republic
during the winter Chan week, I went up to the abbot’s quarters to ask for instruction.
My grandteacher asked me: “What method do you apply?”
I said: “I also recite the Buddha’s name, and also practice Chan — the dual practice of Chan and the Pure Land.”
He asked: “Since you recite the Buddha’s name, how can you practice Chan?”

I said: “When I recite the Buddha’s name, within the meaning there is the doubt of who it is who recites the Buddha’s name; and thus, though I am reciting the Buddha’s name, I am also practicing Chan.”

He asked: “Do deluded thoughts arise or not?” I answered: “When the right thought is raised, deluded thoughts also often follow along behind. When the right thought is set down, there are no deluded thoughts either — pure and at ease.”

My grandteacher said: “This ‘pure and at ease’ is laziness and laxity — soaking a stone in cold water; cultivate for a thousand years and all is spent in vain. You must surely raise the right thought, bravely investigate, and see clearly who it is who at bottom recites the Buddha’s name; only then can you break through the Chan barrier. You must practice with vigor.”
I asked: “I hear that the grandteacher, on Mount Zhongnan, entered samadhi for eighteen days — did he enter it with mind, or without mind?”

He answered: “To enter samadhi with a mind, one can certainly not be still. To enter samadhi without a mind is like a clay or wooden statue. Restraining the mind to one place, there is nothing that is not accomplished.”
I asked: “I want to learn my grandteacher’s samadhi; I beg the grandteacher to transmit it.”
He answered: “It is impossible without looking at the huatou.”
I asked: “What is called a huatou?”
He answered: “‘Hua’ is deluded thought — talking to oneself.
At the place where deluded thoughts have not yet arisen, contemplate, and see what the original face is; this is called looking at the huatou.

When deluded thoughts have already arisen, still raise the right thought, and the wrong thought dies of itself. If one turns along with deluded thought, sitting in meditation is of no use. If one raises the right thought but it is not earnest, the huatou has no strength and deluded thought will surely arise. Hence in applying effort one must be brave and vigorous, as one mourning a father and mother. The ancients said: “Studying the Way is like guarding a city — grip the city wall and hold it for a while; without once enduring the cold that cuts to the bone, how can one get the plum blossom’s fragrance to fill one’s nose?” (These words my grandteacher spoke at every Chan week.)
If there are no deluded thoughts, there is also no huatou; with an empty mind one sits in stillness, soaking a stone in cold water — sit on for immeasurable kalpas and there is no benefit.

As for Chan practice, if one is not going to practice it, that is all; but once one has resolved to practice, one must be brave and vigorous, like one man fighting ten thousand, pressing straight ahead without retreat, nor loosening the grip. Reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise so, and holding a mantra is likewise so; make the thought of birth and death urgent, pressing tighter day by day, and the effort will make progress.”

blocks.text: Tending the Huatou and Turning the Hearing Back to Hear the Self-Nature

inline.s: Excerpted from Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions · the Chan Hall Instructions

What is a huatou? Hua is to speak, and tou is before speaking. For instance, reciting “Amitabha Buddha” is a spoken phrase; before it is spoken is the huatou. The so-called huatou is the moment when a single thought has not yet arisen; the instant a thought arises, it has already become the huashu. This moment when a thought has not yet arisen is called non-arising; not scattered, not drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness — that is called non-ceasing. At every moment, with a single solitary thought, turn the light back and shine upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing” — this is called looking at the huatou, or tending the huatou.

[Non-arising and non-ceasing] The “non-arising and non-ceasing” spoken of here is: a single thought does not arise, and the probing does not cease (not scattered, not drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness). [Scattered] The agitation of the thought-mind.
Someone asked
(a person asked)
: “As for the Bodhisattva Guanyin’s turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature — how is this seen to be Chan practice?”

[Turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature is Chan practice] In the Chan Hall Instructions, Old Master Xuyun, when speaking of the method of Chan practice, said: “Though there are many methods of practice, all the Buddhas and patriarchs take Chan practice as the supreme wonderful gate. In the Shurangama assembly, the Buddha commanded Bodhisattva Manjushri to select the perfect penetration, and took the Bodhisattva Guanyin’s ear-root perfect penetration as foremost. When we turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, that is Chan practice.”
I
(just now)
said that tending the huatou is teaching you, at every moment, with a single solitary thought, to turn the light back and shine upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing.”
Turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature is likewise teaching you, at every moment, with a single solitary thought, to turn the hearing back and hear the self-nature.

‘Turn’ is to reverse, and “non-arising and non-ceasing” is the self-nature. ‘Hear’ and ‘reflect’, when one goes with the stream, follow sound and chase form: hearing does not go beyond sound, seeing does not transcend form, and discrimination is obvious. But when one turns against the stream and contemplates the self-nature, no longer following sound and chasing form, then it is originally a single essence of clarity, and ‘hearing’ and ‘reflecting’ are not two different things. We should know that what is called tending the huatou and what is called turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature are by no means to be done with the eyes, nor to be heard with the ears. If one uses the eyes to look, or the ears to listen, that is following sound and chasing form, turned by objects — this is called going with the stream. If a single solitary thought rests in “non-arising and non-ceasing,” not following sound and not chasing form, this is called turning against the stream, called tending the huatou, and also called turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature.

[Turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature] The Shurangama Sutra says: “Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.” Concerning turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature, in the Essentials of Mind-Cultivation there is a passage of most splendid discussion: “Since there are many ways in which one enters the principle, I shall point out to you one gate, that you may return to the source. Do you still hear the sound of the crow cawing and the magpie chattering? He said: I hear. He said: Turn your hearing back to hear your hearing-nature. Is there still any sound? He said: Coming to this, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely ungraspable. He said: Wonderful! Wonderful! This is Guanyin’s gate of entering the principle. I will ask you further: you say, ‘coming to this, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely ungraspable.’ Since they are ungraspable, at that moment is it empty space? He said: It turns out it is not empty, bright and not dim. He said: What is the substance of this not-empty? He said: It has no appearance either; words cannot reach it. He said: This is the life of all the Buddhas and all the patriarchs; doubt it no more.” [A single essence of clarity] Refers to the self-nature pure mind originally inherent in everyone. “Clarity” describes its bright and supremely subtle purity. The Shurangama Sutra says: “Originally, relying on a single essence of clarity, it divides into six harmonious unions.” A single essence of clarity is the one mind. The six harmonious unions are the six faculties harmoniously uniting with the six dusts: the eye uniting with form, the ear with sound, the nose with fragrance, the tongue with taste, the body with touch, and the mind with objects.
Excerpted from Old Master Xuyun’s Letters on Chan
I often grieve that the Dharma gate
(the Chan gate)
has fallen away, and that good friends
(good and wise friends
are rarely heard of. Yet students are as numerous as the hairs of an ox
(a metaphor for very many)
, while those who accomplish are like the horns of a rabbit
(a metaphor for there being not one)
. This is because they themselves do not possess the eyes and ears
(because their reasoning is unclear)

, and have lost the art of good tuning. Hence the ancients said: for one to look at the huatou, he must let go his whole body, like a dead man, and singly raise this one thought to probe forward, arousing the doubt.
Doubt what? Since it is called a huatou, it has already fallen into the huashu. One should know that a true huatou
must be probed toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted
. Apart from movement and stillness, thought after thought unbroken —
this is called the doubt

(Apart from movement and stillness, probing thought after thought, unbroken, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted — this is called the doubt. Note: here the “doubt” is the doubt of looking at the huatou; the “doubt” spoken of in the preceding section, “The Huatou and the Doubt,” is the doubt of probing the huashu.)
Doubt on and doubt on, until it is beaten into one mass.
(After the doubt has beaten into a single mass, )
turn the light back once and shine — who is this doubter? Time after time, when the melon is ripe the stem falls, and suddenly one touches the nostrils one was born with
(penetrating through to see the nature)
, not obtained from outside.

[Since it is called a huatou, it has already fallen into the huashu] To think that a phrase or a word is the huatou, and yet it is actually already the huashu. In the Chan Hall Instructions, Old Master Xuyun said: “The so-called huatou is the moment when a single thought has not yet arisen; the instant a thought arises, it has already become the huashu.” [The three-stage progression of Chan] One:

probe toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted, and beat the doubt into a single mass; two: turn the light back once and shine — who is this doubter? three: (time after time) when the melon ripens the stem falls, and one penetrates through to see the nature.
Hence the ancestral founder of Yongjia
(Master Yongjia)

said: “Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; in speech and silence, in movement and stillness, the body is at peace.” Practicing thus, what difficulty is there? Where can sickness arise? The so-called “wild mind” is the various poisons from of old. One should know that in the school a single word is of no use — Buddha and Mara are both beheaded.

[Various poisons] All views, high-sounding words, and beautiful sayings. Master Hanshan said: “The method of applying the mind is to raise alone the one thought leading upward, and to stand firmly with your heels planted at the very place where the Buddhas and patriarchs do not allow. Next, one must vomit out entirely the manifold views, high-sounding words, and beautiful sayings, the various poisons, in the breast.” (from the Mengyou Collection, instructions to Chan man Shuanglunzhao) He also said: “This matter (seeing the nature and becoming Buddha) is in everyone originally without want, complete and fully endowed. That daily use does not know it, and one cannot gain its use, is precisely because the seeds of evil habits since beginningless, soaked and dyed over countless kalpas, are deeply rooted and hard to pull out. Now, being newly soaked by the words and letters of the teachings, the gongans of the patriarchs, and all manner of views, adds a further layer of hindrance. Though one seeks to understand oneself, the more one seeks, the further one goes. Why is this? It is only because one has lost sight of oneself and seeks it from others. Because the accumuled afflictions of many lives are called the affliction hindrance, and the subtle-seemingly views are called the hindrance of what is known. If these two hindrances are removed, the original body manifests of itself. Now, in probing the upward matter, one must first vomit out completely all the previously learned words and language, subtle-seeming principles and views — called the various poisons. Raise alone the original huatou of one’s own, place a heavy doubt beneath it, and cut off the root of deluded thought and affliction. Make it so that inside cannot get out, and outside cannot get in. Cut off before and after, and the middle becomes solitary; there is only a single mass of doubt, made into one’s own life-root. Doubt on to the point where one cannot doubt further, to the place where force is of no use; fix the gaze and look — see what at bottom it is? Looking and looking, pressing and pressing, there will of itself be a time of turning back. But if even a hair of view remains in the midst, then it is separated by thousands of miles. Just look at the first patriarch (Damo): “With a mind like a wall, one may enter the Way” — this is the first road home. If the mind will not die, and the doubt is not rightly weighted, then for a thousand births and a hundred kalpas one is at last on the road. Mountain master, draw your spirit into this, and you may be sure that the attainment you will gain some day is not something that ‘zhizhezhe’ clever talk can reach. Do take care, again and again!” (from the Mengyou Collection, instructions to Master Zhixixian) [Turning back] The outcome, the conclusion. Here it means penetrating through to see the nature.

What is spoken of as movement and stillness, the beginning student cannot but investigate. Walking, standing, the hall, the work, welcoming and seeing off, talking and laughing, urine and excrement and the like are called movement; sitting and lying in quiet tranquility is called stillness. Thus, searching minutely
(one must search thus minutely)
: now, in the six periods of the day and night
(I now, within twenty-four hours)
, after all when am I in movement, and do not follow the movement away
(still probing toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? When am I in stillness, and am not turned by the stillness
(still probing toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? Facing all states, does thought arise or not? If one can truly examine as before
(if one is truly able to examine thus)
, in movement not following the movement away
(in movement not giving rise to deluded thought)
, then one is able to be alert and still
(then able to be alert and still)
; in stillness not being turned by the stillness
(in stillness not falling into drowsiness)
, then one is still and alert
(then still and alert)

This is merely your initial awareness. In movement and stillness do not veer to one side; surely movement and stillness become one, matter and principle perfectly merge. As is justly said by the twenty-seventh patriarch
(the Venerable Prajnatara, the twenty-seventh patriarch of the Western Land, the master of the first patriarch Damo)
: “The in-breath does not rest in the skandhas and realms; the out-breath does not touch the manifold conditions. Always turning thus the sutra — a hundred, a thousand, a million kotis of scrolls.”

[Skandhas and realms] The five skandhas and the eighteen realms. [The five skandhas] The old translation of the five aggregates; “skandha” has the meaning of veiling, being able to veil the true Thusness Dharma-nature and give rise to various afflictions. [The five aggregates] The form aggregate, feeling aggregate, perception aggregate, volition aggregate, and consciousness aggregate — the five great elements that constitute the human body. The form aggregate is the body; the feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness aggregates are the mind. [The eighteen realms] The combining of the six faculties — eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — the six dusts — form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharma — and the six consciousnesses — eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness — is called the “eighteen realms.”

[The in-breath does not rest in the skandhas and realms; the out-breath does not touch the manifold conditions] This is mutual-embedded wording, meaning: the in-breath (inhaling) and the out-breath (exhaling) are not deluded by body and mind; the in-breath and out-breath are not deluded by circumstances. That is, at no time is one deluded by body and mind or by circumstances. [Mutual-embedded wording] Mutual-embedded wording, also called mutual phrasing, is a rhetorical method often used in classical Chinese. Its characteristic is that it is not verbose, not cumbersome, not flat and prosaic; it is subtle and concentrated, economizing words while keeping the meaning, complementing each other to convey the sense, and casting light upon each other. For example, in the Ballad of Mulan, “the general and the soldier fought to the death in a hundred battles; the general and the soldier returned after ten years.” Another example, from the Record of the Yueyang Tower, “not rejoicing over external things, not grieving over oneself,” meaning: not rejoicing because of external things and oneself, and also not grieving because of external things and oneself. Here “external things” refers to other people and one’s circumstances, and “oneself” refers to one’s own lot.

[The in-breath does not rest in the skandhas and realms; the out-breath does not touch the manifold conditions; always turning thus the sutra — a hundred, a thousand, a million kotis of scrolls] The in-breath and out-breath not deluded by body and mind, the in-breath and out-breath not deluded by circumstances; always chanting such a sutra (taking the reality-mark as the sutra) is equal to chanting a hundred, a thousand, a million kotis of scrolls of sutra. The Congrong Record says: “The king of eastern India invited the twenty-seventh patriarch Prajnatara. During the meal, the king asked: ‘Why do you not read the sutras?’ The patriarch said: ‘This poor monk’s in-breath does not rest in the skandhas and realms; his out-breath does not touch the manifold conditions; always he turns such a sutra — a hundred, a thousand, a million kotis of scrolls.’” [Turning the sutra] Reciting the sutra. The Biographies of Eminent Monks, in the treatise on sutra specialists, says: “Chanting the sutra is called turning and reading; singing praises is called Brahma sound.” [During the meal] In the midst of the meal. “Secondary” has the meaning of “amidst”: as the chest is called the midst of the breast, and the table is called the midst of the seats.
Inconceivable
(do not go to think about it; in Chan practice one must not use the consciousness mind to ponder, gauge, and argue)

— do not on any account seek after words and follow the turning of another’s tongue, exhausting your spirit with no real benefit. Sit on the meditation cushion and you doze and grow drowsy; set your legs down and you chatter idly; encountering circumstances and sounds
(conditions)
, you have not a whit of mastery. What a misfortune! Each of you should be on your guard.
Note: Old Master Xuyun’s Letters on Chan was originally published in the tenth year, fourth issue, of the Haichao Voice; it should be
or thereabouts, a letter Old Master Xuyun wrote to his disciple Master Xiuyuan, instructing him on looking at the huatou.

blocks.text: The Two Kinds of Difficulty and Ease in Applying Effort

inline.s: For one who applies effort and cultivates the Way, according to the depth of his effort, there are two kinds of difficulty and ease: one, the difficulty and ease of beginning the effort; two, the difficulty and ease of having long applied the effort.

blocks.text: One: The Difficulty and Ease of Beginning the Effort

inline.s: [The thieving mind] The clinging mind. Because the clinging mind steals the Dharma-wealth, keeping the true Dharma from manifesting, the Chan grove calls it the thieving mind. The An (
ǎn
) Black Bean Collection says:
“The thieving mind not dying is the great ailment of the student.”

[The clinging mind] The mind that clings to the six dusts and arises, also called the deliberating mind. [Dharma-wealth] The counterpart of “worldly wealth”; it refers to the Buddha-Dharma. Because the Buddha-Dharma can nourish sentient beings, being the provisions by which they grow the life of wisdom, like the precious things of the world, it is figuratively called Dharma-wealth.

The common ailment of the beginning practitioner is that deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies will not let go: ignorance and pride, jealousy and obstruction, greed, anger, and deluded love, laziness and love of good food, what is right and wrong, self and others — all swelling up a full belly. How can that accord with the Way?
[Pride] Arrogance and conceit.

There are those who come from a pampered young-master background, whose habits of indulgence they cannot forget, who cannot bear the least grievance, cannot taste the least hardship — how can they apply effort and cultivate the Way? They have not reflected on what sort of person the original teacher Shakyamuni Buddha was when he left home.
There are some who have read a few characters, but do not know that the questions in the records of the ancients are meant to test the depth of the student
(are meant to examine and test the depth of the student’s effort)

; so they make themselves clever, spending their days hunting phrases, discoursing on mind and on Buddha, interpreting the ancients’ words and sentences as doctrine, doing this business of counting another’s food and treasures, and still thinking themselves remarkable, giving rise to great pride. When they meet with a great illness, they cry out to heaven and earth; or when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives
(or when death arrives)
, they are all in a fluster; the understanding of their whole life is of no use at all, and only then do they regret it too late.

There is more, a kind of person who distorts the saying “fundamentally Buddha, not belonging to cultivation and realization.” He says it is originally already perfected and there is no need to cultivate or realize; all day he is idle and loose, indulging his feelings and letting go. Wasting the light, he yet calls himself “a person beyond the pattern, free and easy according to conditions.” Such a person will eat a great deal of bitterness.
One who has a little resolve for the Way, on the other hand, cannot grasp hold of a place to begin.

There are those who fear deluded thoughts, and try to get rid of them but cannot; all day they are fretful and anxious, blaming themselves that their karmic hindrances are deep, and so lose their resolve for the Way.

There are those who want to fight deluded thoughts to the death; in a blaze of anger they clench their fists and puff themselves up, puff out their chests and stare, as if in all earnestness, about to wage a war to the death with deluded thoughts. Little do they know that deluded thoughts cannot be fought off, and instead they end up spitting blood and going mad.
There are those who fear falling into emptiness; little do they know that a “ghost” has already been produced, and that emptiness cannot be emptied out, nor can they awaken.

There are those who use the mind to seek awakening; little do they know that seeking to awaken to the Way and wishing to become Buddha are all a great deluded thought — sand is not the substance of rice
(boiling sand cannot make rice)
, and though one seek to the “Year of the Donkey,” one will certainly not awaken.

There are those who, encountering one or two sticks of still incense, give rise to a joyful mind; that is only a blind turtle praising a hole in a log — happening upon it by chance, not real effort; and it adds another layer of the joy-hindrance.
[One or two sticks of still incense] In these one or two sticks of incense, the mind is clear and quiet.
There are those who, in stillness, find it clear and pure and very comfortable; but in movement it won’t do; so they flee the noisy toward the quiet, and sit in dead water passing their days.
Matters such as these are many, very many.
When the beginning practitioner cannot find the road it is truly hard: with awareness but no reflection, one is scattered and cannot “settle into the hall”
(that is, the mind is scattered and the effort cannot settle into the hall)
; with reflection but no awareness, one again sits and drowns in dead water.

Though it is said to be hard, once one finds the road it is very easy. What is the ease of the beginning? There is no cleverness to it; just put it down. Put down what? Just put down the whole mass of ignorance and affliction.

Fellow meditators! When this body of ours is breathless for a single moment, it is a corpse. The reason we cannot put it down is only that we have taken it as precious, and thus have given rise to self and others, right and wrong, love and hate, grasping and rejecting. If one is clear that this body is a corpse, does not treasure it, and does not at all regard it as oneself, what then is there that one cannot put down?

If only one can put it down, then at every time, in every place, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, moving or still, busy or idle, inside and outside the whole body, cold and still, there is only a single doubt-thought, even and gentle, probing on without break, without a speck of another thought mixed in; a single huatou, like a heaven-propped long sword — whoever touches its edge is blotted out and silent. What deluded thoughts then need be feared? What is there that can strike you down at leisure? Who will then distinguish movement from stillness? Who will then cling to existence or emptiness?

If one fears deluded thoughts, that adds another layer of deluded thought; to be aware of purity, is already not purity; to fear falling into emptiness, is already to have fallen into existence; to wish to become Buddha, is already to have entered the path of Mara.
Therefore, if only one recognizes the road
(the road is just this single thought of putting everything down and raising the huatou alone)

, then carrying water and hauling firewood are all the wonderful Way, and hoeing the fields and planting the ground are all the Chan machine; it is not that only by sitting cross-legged on a cushion all day is one counted as applying effort and cultivating the Way.
